t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we will study methods of detecting barbiturates. The aim is to teach the general and microcrystalloscopic, that is specific, reactions for barbiturates, and the conditions for crystal formation. The plan has two items. First, derivatives of barbituric acid, their physicochemical properties, narcological significance, microcrystalloscopic analysis and colour reactions. Second, isolation of barbiturates from physical evidence and their analysis by TLC screening, UV spectrophotometry and other physicochemical methods.

Reagents and equipment. For colour reactions, filter paper impregnated with cobalt nitrate, ammonia vapour, and alcoholic solutions of cobalt acetate and isopropylamine are needed. For microcrystalloscopy, a microscope slide, a microscope, a moist chamber, that is a Petri dish, concentrated sulphuric acid and copper-pyridine reagent are used. In TLC, chloroform-n-butanol-25% ammonia in the ratio 70:40:5, diphenylcarbazone and mercury sulphate are used. For UV spectrophotometry, 0.05 M borate buffer and 1 M alkali are needed.

Safety rules. The student brings rubber gloves, a wipe and a face mask to the laboratory work. The examination is carried out in rooms with ventilation and a fume cupboard. After the work such rooms are locked and sealed. Objects from persons with infectious diseases, that is tuberculosis, hepatitis or AIDS, arrive in a special container and are marked in the documents.

General description of barbiturates. Barbituric acid, that is malonylurea, is not used in medicine. Its derivatives, the barbiturates, are widely used and have great narcological significance. In medicine they are used as sedatives, hypnotics, anaesthetic agents and anticonvulsants, and they also show addictive properties. More than 2500 barbiturates have been obtained by synthesis from malonic acid and urea. At present more than 50 of them are used in medicine worldwide.

t: Lethal dose and elimination: the numbers
n: Lethal dose and elimination. The lethal dose of barbiturates is 20 times the therapeutic dose. For barbital this is 6-10 g, for phenobarbital 4-6 g. In healthy people, 70-80% of barbital and 15-20% of phenobarbital is excreted in the urine. The persistence of barbiturates in biological objects is reported as from 1.5 months to 14 months.

The pKa values and molecular mass of barbiturates. Barbiturates are substances of acidic nature; pKa values range from about 7.4 to 8.0. Phenobarbital has pKa 7.4 and molecular mass 232.2. Barbital has pKa 8.0 and molecular mass 184.2. Allobarbital has pKa 7.8; amobarbital and butalbital pKa 7.9; cyclobarbital pKa 7.6.

t: Solubility of barbiturates: water and ethanol
n: Solubility of barbiturates. Barbital dissolves in water at 1:130 and in ethanol at 1:14. Phenobarbital in water 1:1000, in ethanol 1:8. Amobarbital in water 1:1300, in ethanol 1:15. Cyclobarbital in water 1:800, in ethanol 1:5. Pentobarbital dissolves in ethanol at 1:4.5 and is very slightly soluble in water. That is, all of them dissolve better in ethanol than in water.

International and national control. Under the 1971 UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 12 barbiturates are under control. Under Resolution No. 330 of the Cabinet of Ministers of Uzbekistan of 12 November 2015, 13 types of barbiturate are listed. In the Convention schedules, secobarbital is in Schedule II; amobarbital, butalbital and 2 others are in Schedule III; and allobarbital, barbital and phenobarbital are in Schedule IV.

Physical properties. All barbiturates, except thiopental sodium, are solid crystalline, odourless substances with a bitter taste. They dissolve well in diethyl ether, less well in chloroform and alcohol, and poorly in water. At high temperature they undergo dry distillation, that is they sublime. The sublimate crystals are characteristic of some barbiturates.

Let us compare barbital and phenobarbital. Both belong to the group of long-acting barbiturates. Synonyms of barbital: Veronal, Malonal, Sonal; synonyms of phenobarbital: Phenemal, Phenobarbital. The molecular mass of barbital is 184.2 and pKa 8.0; that of phenobarbital is 232.2 and pKa 7.4. In urine, 70-80% of barbital and 15-20% of phenobarbital is excreted.

Melting point of some barbiturates. If the residue is large or the evidence is a pure powder, the first test is to determine the melting point. Barbital melts at 189-191 °C, phenobarbital at 174-177 °C, barbamyl at 141 °C, hexenal at 143-146 °C. Thiopental, that is the sodium salt, melts at 156-159 °C; it is white, sometimes yellowish, with a faint odour characteristic of sulphur.

Thiopental sodium and barbital sodium. Both are neutral rather than acidic in nature. Thiopental sodium is white, sometimes yellowish, with a sulphurous odour; melting point 156-159 °C; it is insoluble in diethyl ether. Barbital sodium dissolves in water at 1:5, in hot water at 1:2.5 and in ethanol at 1:400; melting point 190 °C. Remember: unlike the free barbiturates, these salts are neutral.

Groups by hypnotic action. By their hypnotic action, barbiturates are divided into three groups. Long-acting: barbital and phenobarbital. Intermediate-acting: barbamyl and etaminal. Short-acting: hexenal and butobarbital. At present barbital, phenobarbital, hexenal, barbamyl, etaminal, benzonal and butobarbital are used in medicine.

Toxicological significance. The lethal dose of barbiturates is 20 times the therapeutic dose. The lethal dose is 6-10 g for barbital and 4-6 g for phenobarbital. Some of them accumulate. In death, pathological examination shows no characteristic signs. For this reason, in poisoning, forensic chemical analysis of the biological object and, above all, determination of the quantity of the substance are of great importance.

Metabolism and excretion. In the body, barbiturates undergo dealkylation, hydroxylation and carboxylation. Part is detoxified in the liver and part is excreted in the urine. Of the barbital taken, 70-80% is excreted in the urine, and 15-20% of phenobarbital, which is why urine is examined. Long-acting drugs are little broken down in the liver and are excreted in the urine; short-acting ones such as hexenal and thiopental are rapidly broken down in the liver. Persistence in biological objects, according to different authors, is from 1.5 months to 14 months.

Signs of poisoning. The patient sleeps for a long time, sometimes not waking for 1-2 days, and breathes with snoring. Blood pressure falls, the limbs become cold, and sometimes there is nausea and vomiting. Death occurs from paralysis of the centres that control breathing and the blood vessels.

Isolation methods. Barbiturates are isolated from the object by the acidified alcohol or acidified water method; some by specific methods. From biological fluids they are extracted with organic solvents. In the acidification methods, barbiturates, neutral substances such as phenacetin, and alkaloids with weakly basic properties are tested for in the acidic isolate.

Purification of the isolate. Substances with acidic properties, that is organic acids and barbiturates, are purified by re-extraction with alkali at pH 13 and acid at pH 1. Dry distillation, that is sublimation, is used for sublimable substances such as barbiturates, benzoic and salicylic acids and caffeine. Chromatographic methods give an analysis of identity as well as purification from foreign substances.

General reactions, the first with alkali. If the residue is large or the physical evidence is a pure powder, the melting point is determined first. Barbiturates are stable to acids and alkalis. When heated with alkali at high temperature, they decompose and an odour of ammonia is noticed. If acid is added to the reaction product, the odour of the corresponding acid is noticed. All barbiturates give this reaction.

The scheme for selecting general reactions. If the residue is large or the evidence is a pure powder, the melting point is determined and the reaction with alkali is carried out, in which an odour of ammonia is noticed. Small quantities of barbiturates are detected by colour reactions: isonitrosobarbituric acid, cobalt ammoniate, cobalt-isopropylamine. Microcrystalloscopic reactions are carried out with concentrated H2SO4 and copper-pyridine reagent.

The isonitrosobarbituric acid reaction. Perhydrol and ammonium chloride are added to the barbiturate residue and heated; an oxidation product forms. With Na2S, barbituric acid is formed. With nitrites, red isonitrosobarbituric acid is formed. With iron salts it gives a blue iron complex. That is, the colour changes from red to blue.

Cobalt reactions for small quantities. Small quantities of barbiturates are detected by general reactions; cobalt reactions are among them. A drop of the alcoholic isolate is placed on paper impregnated with cobalt nitrate and exposed to ammonia vapour. The cobalt salt with NH3 and methyl alcohol gives a characteristic red colour. Cobalt acetate with isopropylamine forms a red-pink colour and an inner complex compound. Interfering: purine alkaloids and substances containing a biuret chain.

t: Scheme of the reaction with cobalt ammoniate
n: The reaction with cobalt ammoniate. Filter paper impregnated with cobalt nitrate is soaked with an alcoholic solution containing the barbiturate and exposed to ammonia vapour. All barbiturates form a characteristic red colour with an ammoniacal solution of cobalt salts in the presence of methyl alcohol. The product is an inner complex of cobalt. The reaction is interfered with by purine alkaloids and substances containing a biuret chain.

t: Reaction with cobalt acetate and isopropylamine
n: The reaction with cobalt acetate and isopropylamine. Alcoholic solutions of cobalt acetate and isopropylamine are added to the chloroform solution and shaken. If barbiturates are present, a red-pink colour and a red inner complex compound are formed.

Basics of microcrystalloscopy. The method is based on identification by the structure, size and colour of the crystals. The substance is placed on a microscope slide, a drop of reagent is added, and the crystals are examined. Advantages: a very small amount of substance is sufficient; the method is used in the analysis of explosive and poisonous substances; no filtration, evaporation or heating is required. The crystals should be 20-50 μm; particles of 2-20 μm are examined at a magnification of 150-250 times.

The steps of microcrystalloscopy. The substance under test is placed on a microscope slide, then a drop of reagent is added and the crystals are examined under the microscope. The crystals formed should be 20-50 μm in size; particles of 2-20 μm are examined at a magnification of 150-250 times. If the reaction is slow, the slide is placed in a Petri dish with moistened filter paper, that is, in a moist chamber. Under the microscope, attention is paid to the shape, faces and colour of the crystals.

Conditions of crystallisation. In crystallisation, a crystallisation centre forms first, then the crystal grows. If the first stage is slow, large crystals form. For large crystals, the reagent is allowed to act on dilute and hot solutions. From concentrated solutions, on the other hand, small crystals without a characteristic form separate out. Crystallisation begins at the edges of the drop; if the reaction is slow, the slide is placed in a moist chamber.

Let us compare the conditions of crystallisation. If the first stage is slow, there are few crystallisation centres, but the crystals are large. In this case the reagent acts on dilute and hot solutions. Conversely, if a concentrated reagent acts on a concentrated solution, there are many centres and small crystals without a characteristic form are formed.

Disadvantages of the method. Often crystals of a definite shape may fail to form. Causes: concentration of the substance and reagent, volume, rate of crystal formation, evaporation, pH, temperature, polymorphism. Many substances give similar crystals, which reduces specificity. For a correct conclusion, a comparison control is carried out.

Microcrystalloscopic reactions of barbiturates. With sulphuric acid: the residue is dissolved in concentrated H2SO4 and, when diluted with water, a white turbidity forms. The precipitate crystals of most barbiturates have a characteristic shape. Copper-pyridine reagent gives an amorphous or crystalline precipitate. The compound formed is decomposed by mineral acids.

The copper-pyridine reaction. If copper-pyridine reagent is added to a residue containing a barbiturate, an amorphous or crystalline precipitate forms. The reaction is carried out on a microscope slide; a copper salt and pyridine take part. The compound formed is decomposed by mineral acids.

TLC screening. The mobile phase is chloroform-n-butanol-25% ammonia in the ratio 70:40:5. The residue is dissolved in chloroform and spotted on the plate. Developing reagents: a chloroform solution of diphenylcarbazone and an aqueous solution of mercury sulphate are sprayed on. Barbiturates form a blue-violet spot with a characteristic Rf value.

Basics of UV spectrophotometry. In the keto, that is acidic, form, barbiturates give no characteristic maximum in the UV region. In borate buffer, 0.05 M, pH 9.2, in the monoimide form they give a spectral maximum at 239-241 nm. In 1 M alkali, pH 13, in the diimide form they give a maximum at 254-256 nm. That is, when the medium changes, both the form of the barbiturate and the maximum change.

UV spectra of commonly used barbiturates. The wavelength of the maximum is in nm; the specific absorbance A, 1%, 1 cm, is given in brackets. Barbital at pH 9.2: 239 nm, 549, at pH 13: 254 nm, 427. Phenobarbital: 239 nm, 452, and 254 nm, 342. Amobarbital: 240 nm, 445, and 255 nm, 364. Pentobarbital: 239 nm, 438, and 255 nm, 327. The table gives the UV, IR and mass spectral data of 12 barbiturates.

UV spectra of other barbiturates. Allobarbital at pH 9.2: 241 nm, 460, at pH 13: 256 nm, 356. Butobarbital: 239 nm, 477, and 254 nm, 388. Cyclobarbital: 239 nm, 410, and 256 nm, 320. Secbutabarbital: 239 nm, 428, and 254 nm, 354. For vinylbital in aqueous alkali, 247 nm, A=298, is given. The identity of barbiturates can be assessed by comparing the spectra in two media, at pH 9.2 and pH 13.

Gas chromatography conditions. The column is glass, 2 m long, with an internal diameter of 2-4 mm. The sorbent is 3% SE-30 on Chromosorb G-HP. The mobile phase is nitrogen, 45-50 ml/min. The mode is isothermal, column temperature 190-200 °C. Injector and detector temperature 220 °C. Barbiturates are identified by retention indices and the Kovats index.

HPLC conditions. The column is 150 mm, internal diameter 2.6 mm, packed with octadecyl silica gel. Mobile phase: 0.1 M phosphate buffer of pH 3.5 and methanol in the ratio 60:40. Flow rate 2 ml/min. The detector is a UV spectrometer, detecting at 216 nm. 20 μl of sample is injected.

Interpreting the result and limitations. The cobalt reaction is interfered with by purine alkaloids and substances containing a biuret chain. In microcrystalloscopy many substances give similar crystals, that is, specificity is low, so a comparison control is needed. In barbiturate poisoning there are no pathological signs, so determination of the quantity of the substance is essential.

Review questions. First, the toxicological and narcological significance of barbituric acid derivatives and the specific methods of isolating them from the object. Second, the general reactions, the equation of the reaction of cobalt salt and ammonia, and microcrystalloscopic reactions. Third, the 1971 UN Convention, grouping by hypnotic action, signs of poisoning, and the TLC method. Fourth, the essence of UV spectrophotometry, the effect of the medium, determination of identity and quantity, and differential spectrophotometry.

Conclusion. General reactions: melting point, odour of ammonia with alkali, isonitrosobarbituric acid, red to blue, and cobalt, red. In microcrystalloscopy, concentrated H2SO4 and copper-pyridine; in TLC, chloroform-n-butanol-NH3, 70:40:5, blue-violet spot. UV spectrophotometry: 239-241 nm at pH 9.2, 254-256 nm at pH 13. GC and HPLC conditions are given separately.
